#1114. Why Liverpool have a point to prove against Man United: Andoni Iraola's side must end rotten run against 'Big Six' rivals - and Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak have to finally step up when it matters

Published: 01:42 EST, 22 November 2026 | Updated: 06:50 EST, 22 November 2026

Given the carousel of chaos and never-ending crises at Old Trafford, it is easy to forget there are football storylines away from the headline-generating machine of Manchester United and Mauricio Pochettino.

Lo and behold, there is – and Liverpool also enter Sunday’s clash against the old enemy with a point to prove.

One problem for Andoni Iraola is his side's frailties in the bigger games, which comes into focus this weekend with United in town – despite the desire to make an easy joke about how this is a clash against relegation fodder.

Since thrashing United 7-0 in 2023, Liverpool have beaten their friends in Manchester just once in seven meetings, including two draws and a defeat at Anfield.

To use a cliche, form seems to go out of the window for this fixture. In the last two Anfield meetings, Liverpool have been first and second in the table, United 14th and then tenth. This weekend, it is fourth against 18th, though Pochettino’s side could be bottom by kick-off.

Liverpool’s struggles in bigger games stretch further. Against the so-called 'Big Six’, the Reds have won just two of 12 games since winning the Premier League title. In a ‘mini league’ of those six sides, Liverpool are bottom in the aforementioned period.

Andoni Iraola's Liverpool side must prove on Sunday they can deliver in the biggest matches

Manchester United did the double over Liverpool in the Premier League last season

United did the double over Liverpool last season, Manchester City have beaten them four times in little over 12 months, Arsenal won on Merseyside a month ago.

So why has this team gone from looking formidable 18 months ago to rather flappable whenever the historic big boys are in town? Casual neutrals who only tune in for the showpiece Sunday 4.30pm may joke that they have not seen Liverpool play well for a good year.

A lot of the answer to that question comes back to Arne Slot and the issues we documented every week last season, when his side were dull and boring to watch, naked in defence and would capitulate in an instant.

Maybe players like Isak, Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola thrive more in intricate spaces rather than the gaping gaps left behind by the attack-minded bigger teams.

Another reason could be the simple fact that these sides are more likely to expose Liverpool’s vulnerabilities, such as the lack of a true defensive midfielder, the poor full backs or the frailties at defending set-pieces.

Anfield has lost its fear factor somewhat, too. Liverpool are top of the Premier League away table with 13 points from 15, but 18th in the home table with just one win in five games.

City had not won in front of a crowd there since 2003, now they have done it two seasons running. Arsenal had not triumphed at the stadium for 14 years until last month.

Iraola is aware of all this and said on Friday: ‘United finished third in the table last season. You are looking at a squad with exactly the same players. They had very, very good results, especially in the second half of the season.

Liverpool bemoaned Ryan Gravenberch’s red card in their home defeat to Manchester City

The Reds spurned a number of chances when they were beaten 1-0 by Arsenal last month

‘Now we have just started, this is just 10 games. So, for sure, they will be a lot higher in the table (soon). We have to rate them like this and the truth is the reference we have is that they finished third.

‘We have to look at ourselves because we need the points. We need to improve our home form. It is also a big game in terms of relevance. It’s Liverpool v Manchester United, so we want to play well and we want to win.’

Asked if he understands the importance of the fixture to fans, Iraola – who spent the weekend off taking in grassroots football and netball games following his kids – said: ‘I am very aware! This is the biggest one in English football. In this country, this is the one.’

In Iraola’s first two bigger games, a theme threatened to emerge. Against Manchester City, Liverpool were well in the contest until Ryan Gravenberch’s red card but were toothless when it came to putting their chances away, lacking bite in attack.

The game was there to be won at 0-0, with the Anfield crowd roaring, but the Reds did not have the killer instinct to do so.

Against Arsenal, there were plenty of chances to equalise after the Gunners’ early goal but, again, goalkeeper David Raya could have put his feet up and had a cigar. A lot of territory but nothing to make the defence seriously sweat.

In both cases, Liverpool were on the receiving end of refereeing howlers. Gravenberch’s red was not a red – the first yellow should never be a booking – and Alexander Isak had a stonewall penalty turned down. ProRef has admitted errors.

To take a cynical view, though: in the title-winning campaign, we were rarely sat talking about referees or moaning about narrow misses or unfair results. Liverpool found ways to win and had no excuses.

Liverpool need Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak to step up against the league's big boys

And that brings us nicely on to Sunday. It feels like the script has been written for weeks.

Indeed, after United lost 3-0 to Bournemouth and the score was read out to huge cheers at Anfield, Daily Mail Sport wrote: ‘Everyone is looking forward to United sacking Michael Carrick and then rocking up at Anfield to win 1-0 with their new manager in a few weeks.’

It always seems to happen and it feels like United get results against rivals Liverpool and City even when they have felt close to their lowest ebb.

But Liverpool and Iraola must not allow that to happen. There can be no excuses of ‘new manager bounce’, refereeing calls or fine margins come Sunday tea time.

Isak and Wirtz simply must step up. It feels harsh that the pair, Wirtz especially, are always in the spotlight but the £125million and £116million signings have flattered to deceive against the big boys.

Both have been spectacular at times this term but need to show up when it really matters, while £123million addition Barcola is still waiting for his first Premier League goal.

Iraola has history with United. As a player, his Athletic Club side beat Sir Alex Ferguson’s great side 5-3 over two legs in Europe.

‘I said at the time, it was one of the best wins of my career,’ he said. 'United, I remember, were champions of the Premier League, got to the Champions League final and lost to Barcelona the year before. We honestly played much better than them.’

Iraola has remained unbeaten against United into his managerial career, winning two and drawing four of his six meetings with them.

Overall, the former Bournemouth boss has played 38 games against ‘Big Six’ teams in the league: winning ten, drawing ten, losing 18.

But a win is all that matters on Sunday and it is a chance for Liverpool to set the tempo ahead of a busy festive schedule. After already taking on the current top three, Iraola now contests two rivalries with a trip across the city to Everton next week.

Six of nine pre-Christmas games are at Anfield so there is a real chance to build a head of steam in the league, qualify for the next stage of Europe and get to the Carabao Cup semi-final.

Iraola would welcome those festive gifts but, for Liverpool fans, nothing will be sweeter than giving their old foes a good old walloping on Sunday.

#1113. Gyokeres the creator and executioner to see nervous Arsenal past Slavia Prague

With a stylish assist and a gorgeous goal, Viktor Gyokeres produced the sort of match-winning performance that suggests the Swedish striker is making significant progress at last. It has not always been straightforward for him at Arsenal, but this was unquestionably one of his better showings, and it continued an encouraging upturn in his form.

Gyokeres has been the second-choice striker for most of this season, with Mikel Arteta usually preferring the more subtle Kai Havertz in attack. There are signs, though, that Gyokeres is now growing in belief. Following this victory over Slavia Prague, which was much more narrow and nervy than it should have been, he has now scored two goals and registered three assists in his last five appearances.

Even more promising than those statistics was his all-round play in Prague. In the first half especially, Gyokeres held on to long passes, combined with his team-mates and tested the opposition with his runs in behind. For Arsenal’s first goal, he found Noni Madueke with a brilliant pass. For their second, he curled a fabulous strike into the top corner.

“Really good,” said Arteta of Gyokeres. “Not only the assist and the goal, but he was really connected to the team. It’s great news, because I think he needed that performance.”

Those two moments in the first half eventually ensured another European victory for Arteta’s side, but the manager was far from impressed with the second-half showing. So smooth at first, Arsenal became remarkably ragged by the end. Slavia were deserving of their goal, scored by Wiktor Nowak. It looked like complacency had infected the minds of the Arsenal players, and you could feel Arteta’s fury radiating from the touchline.

“We scored two goals and it should have been three, four or five,” said Arteta. “And at half-time the message was clear: there is still a lot to do in this game. Right from the beginning of the second half, we were extremely far from our standards in everything that we have to do, in every basic, in every concept, and in everything we discussed. So much to improve and I take full responsibility for that.”

Without Gabriel Magalhães and David Raya, who both made dramatic stops on the goal-line, this could have become an ugly night for Arsenal against one of the weaker teams in the Champions League. The Czech side have now gone 23 games without a victory in Europe’s premier competition, which equals the longest winless run in European Cup history.

It was a remarkable coincidence that this game fell on November 4, the exact date as the same fixture last season. On that occasion Arsenal were comfortable 3-0 winners, with Mikel Merino scoring twice, and they seemed to be heading towards a similar night when Madueke scored the early opener.

The goal was made by Gyokeres, who held off a defender and then hooked an excellent pass into Madueke’s path. The Arsenal winger had already established his dominance over Oskar Kubiak, his opposite number, and he reached fifth gear before the Polish defender had even reached second. Madueke then slid his finish beneath the body of Nazar Domchak, Slavia’s teenage goalkeeper.

One of Slavia’s many problems in a one-sided first half was their inability to cope with Arsenal’s rotations in midfield. Would Slavia have secured a draw if they had been at full strength? They had been weakened by the banishment of their star striker from the club because of a series of disciplinary failings. Right at the start of the second half we were on the back foot, very sloppy and gave balls away. Then we had to suffer. A lot to learn.

We should have scored more in the first half and if we didn’t do that we had to go and do that in the second half.

We made six changes but we know the quality of the players we have. Whether we were lacking something I don’t know but I would have done the same thing [again].

I value what the team has done now, it is 11 away games we played, but our standards should be higher.

Arteta on Gyokeres: "He was really good. A game we believed was good for him, for the spaces he could use. He was really connected to the team. Great news because I think he needed that. Really pleased."

Arteta: "Two very different halves. The first we played at a really high level. At half-time the message was clear: there is still a lot to do in this game. Right from the beginning we were extremely far from our standards. Very far from the standards we expect from each other."

Maybe they started pressing a bit higher with more intensity. We had too many giveaways especially in the final third. There was too much running from box to box and we have to manage those reactions and go for the third and fourth goal.

Good evening from a chilly Prague, where Arsenal are looking for a repeat of the 3-0 victory they secured here exactly one year ago. It’s a remarkable coincidence that Mikel Arteta’s team have travelled to face Slavia Prague on November 4th in back-to-back years.

On that occasion last year, Max Dowman became the youngest player in Champions League history. He should get more minutes tonight from the bench, given that he is currently suspended from Premier League action following his controversial red card against Fleetwood last week.

That’s the most Arteta has rotated between a Premier League and Champions League game so far this season. Telling perhaps that Konsa, Gabriel and Rice – the team’s defensive bedrock – stay in place. But changes on both sides at full-back, and in the attacking midfield areas.

🔵 𝗧𝗘𝗔𝗠𝙉𝙀𝙒𝙎 🟡 Six changes for our Champions League test 👊

Arsenal’s critics will still grumble about the style of victory, but, of all clubs, this is a team who have no obligation to play in a way that neutrals might enjoy. Arsenal spent so much of Arsene Wenger’s 22-year reign playing football that was mostly stylish but only sometimes effective in big games. Now they are mostly effective but only occasionally stylish on such occasions. If you asked all the travelling fans at Anfield which they prefer, you would receive an overwhelming response.

David Raya has kept a clean sheet in 54% of his Champions League starts (21 clean sheets from 39 starts), the best ratio of any goalkeeper to start at least 25 games in the competition. 🤯🇪🇸 https://t.co/A1Zpn8kJN9

Arsenal return to Slavia Prague for the third time under Mikel Arteta knowing that three points will be another step towards a top-eight finish in the Champions League league phase.

Arteta’s team were 4-0 winners in the Czech capital in a 2021 Europa League quarter-final second leg, and 3-0 victors at this stage of the Champions League a year ago. Bukayo Saka opened the scoring with a penalty before two second-half goals from Mikel Merino.

Paris-St Germain are top of the table on 12 points after their rout against Villarreal last night. Real Madrid, Liverpool and Real Betis are the three teams who have the chance to join them on maximum points. Arsenal will jump to 10 points with a win, above Bayern Munich, Sporting and Aston Villa at a minimum.

Slavia Prague are top of the Czech league and unbeaten after 13 games this season, but they are winless in the Champions League after fixtures against Lens, Sabah and Fernerbahce.

The fixture should be a presentable opportunity for Arteta to rotate his team, especially after a physically taxing game at Anfield where Arsenal showed their mettle to win at Liverpool’s home for the first time since 2012.

Arsenal’s second-string is very strong, though they did not cover themselves in glory at Fleetwood in the League Cup last week when Max Dowman was sent off. Given the 16-year-old is banned for another two Premier League games, and the attention Arteta’s touchline reaction to the red card attracted, one wonders if he might want to seize a chance to put Dowman back on the horse.

William Saliba’s return to full training is very welcome news, despite Ezri Konsa impressing in his absence. Saliba travelled with the squad to Prague, and could make his first appearance of the season following a back injury which flared up in France’s World Cup semi-final against Spain. With fixtures against Manchester City, Borussia Dortmund, Brentford, Spurs, Real Madrid, Bournemouth and Manchester United before the end of 2026 though, they will not want rush him.

Piero Hincapie, Cristhian Mosquera, Martin Zubimendi, Merino, Viktor Gyokeres and Eberechi Eze are other players pushing for greater involvement from the start of matches.

#1112. Anthropic IPO: four ways the AI giant wants to disrupt science

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. Shares in the artificial intelligence firm Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on Thursday, in the biggest initial public offering of all time.Credit: Idrees Mohammed/AFP via Getty

Anthropic, the frontier artificial-intelligence company, has made history with the largest initial public offering (IPO) on record on 19 November. With a staggering valuation of around US$1.5 trillion, the firm, based in San Francisco, California, is now among the world’s most valuable companies — and it has major ambitions in science.

The maker of AI model Claude, Anthropic was founded in 2021 by a group who broke away from rival giant OpenAI. Its models have proven powerful in research, and Anthropic has launched its own directed science effort, focusing on areas including quantum mechanics and protein design. This year alone, it has reported mathematics breakthroughs and launched its first life sciences laboratory.

The IPO might also unleash a historic wave of philanthropy: all seven of Anthropic’s founders are likely to become billionaires and have pledged to donate 80% of their equity in the company to charity, including chief executive Dario Amodei. And on 18 October, the company announced that it had established the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, created to support initiatives that benefit society and stocked with an initial commitment of 5% of Anthropic’s shares.

But the firm has drawn criticism from researchers, who say its aims of curing diseases on short timescales are unrealistic and that its race towards developing ultra-powerful, ‘superintelligent’ AI models pose serious risks, including an existential threat to humanity. In its public prospectus, published ahead of the IPO, Anthropic outlines a new governance structure that it says is “consistent with our commitment to AI safety and responsibility”, and adds that safety research directly shapes the firm’s “model design, training, and deployment.”

Nature looks at four areas of science where Anthropic is making waves.

AI’s potential to turbocharge the discovery of new medicines has been a centerpiece of Anthropic’s pitch to investors. “If today we look at things like cancer, Alzheimer’s, heart disease, mental illness — these will be relics of the past in, I think, less than a decade,” Amodei said in a promotional video ahead of the IPO.

The company has been rapidly expanding its biomedical ambitions. This year, Anthropic opened its first ‘wet’ laboratory for life sciences research, announced partnerships with several pharmaceutical companies, and said it was pursuing drug leads of its own. “We plan to scale this work up substantially from here,” the company said on 27 October.

Anthropic bought a one-person, AI-powered biotech: is this drug discovery’s future?

Anthropic bought a one-person, AI-powered biotech: is this drug discovery’s future?

But Amodei’s habit of promising swift, AI-fueled cures for complex diseases has rankled many researchers and entrepreneurs in the field who feel the timeline is unrealistic.

Over the last year, Anthropic has made a major push in the life sciences. In June, the company hired John Jumper, who shared the 2024 Chemistry Nobel Prize for his work on AlphaFold2 while at Google DeepMind in London.

Some of the company’s early biological research received a mixed reception from biologists. After Anthropic reported using a swarm of AI agents to find signs of a new CRISPR-like system in viral sequence data, some researchers questioned the novelty of the finding and noted that the company had not carried out the experimental work needed to determine the system’s function.

In protein design — a field that has boomed thanks to specialist AI tools including AlphaFold — Anthropic’s work has also failed to generate much excitement. In August, Anthropic used Claude Science — an agentic system that can access other biological tools and databases — to make novel ‘binders’ against 15 protein targets.

“Expectations are sky high,” says Anthony Gitter, a computational biologist at the Morgridge Institute for Research in Madison, Wisconsin. “I understand why some view their initial public results as underwhelming.”

But Gitter is enthusiastic about Anthropic’s protein design efforts, largely because the company was transparent about the work, from the prompts it used to the sequences that were generated. “I would strongly encourage Anthropic to continue that in their future life sciences research,” Gitter adds.

In recent months, Anthropic and other companies — notably Google DeepMind and OpenAI — have been working to establish their research credentials in large part by showing off the rapidly growing mathematical abilities of their flagship AI models.

On 7 September Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge and collaborator Tristan Buckmaster at New York University solved a special case of the Navier-Stokes equations, a long-standing problem in mathematical physics that describes the flow of fluids. Hours after Anthropic announced the result, OpenAI claimed a full solution of the problem, igniting a controversy.

In another collaboration, Alpöge and mathematical physicist Ethan Sussman at Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois, have been working towards establishing the mathematical foundations of the standard model of particle physics. This too is a problem on which OpenAI has made similar claims.

Anthropic and its competitors see the ability to write a rigorous proof of a mathematical fact as a crucial testing ground for their reasoning models. That’s in large part because the correctness of a proof is an objective measure that can be used as a ‘reward’ to further train AI systems.

Liverpool's midfield needs Trey Nyoni, but it might upset a few

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Eighteen months ago, on his first return to Merseyside since leaving the club as manager the summer before, Jurgen Klopp spoke at a charity event at Liverpool Cathedral and singled out Dominik Szoboszlai for praise.

Probably the “best pressing player in Europe right now” was how the German described the Reds’ midfielder, who had played the season in the No. 10 role as Arne Slot’s side swept to the title.

Only nine months ago, Slot described the Hungarian as “maybe the best in the world in terms of pressing.” It’s quite the difference to today, when Szoboszlai’s pressing, now in a deeper role in midfield for Andoni Iraola, is coming into question.

“I think, for me, it’s about, in his mind, managing how much he presses and when to go, as opposed to just pressing for pressing’s sake,” Daniel Sturridge explained during Sky Sports' coverage of the 3-1 win over Crystal Palace.

“I’m not saying that he does that all the time, but I think the reason why Liverpool are open is because they don’t have someone who’s reading in front of the defence.”

That title-winning campaign two seasons ago saw Szoboszlai vital to everything Liverpool did well, with Alexis Mac Allister and Ryan Gravenberch complementing each other - everything was seemingly perfectly balanced. Gravenberch played in a more restricted No. 6 role in front of defence, Mac Allister was the box-to-box No. 8, and Szoboszlai was the all-action, pressing No. 10.

However, Slot worried that opponents had found out how to play against his team, and perhaps aware of losing Trent Alexander-Arnold’s unique creativity from deep, opted for a changed midfield set up. It actually began in the final away game of the title-winning season, away to Brighton, when Szoboszlai started in a two-man midfield alongside Gravenberch.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

And that’s how Slot continued the following campaign, having signed Florian Wirtz for the No. 10 role. It was a move that immediately had its sceptics. Promising Wirtz the central role, where he had never truly played before, seemed to leave Liverpool far more open in midfield.

Szoboszlai, though, became the first Liverpool midfielder since Steven Gerrard to score and assist 10 or more goals in a single campaign, scoring 13 and assisting 12 in 53 games across all competitions. He was named the Reds’ player of the season.

That, though, doesn’t tell the full story. Some fans were irked by the Hungarian’s manner, especially after a heavy defeat at Manchester City. The match-going supporter noticed how often he slowed play down and often encouraged others to do so. Slot saw it differently, saying: “He is an all-round player, an all-round midfielder, a modern midfielder in my opinion. I think this season he has improved his game on the ball. Off the ball, he is top three, four or five in the world.”

With two years left to run on his contract, Szoboszlai was rewarded for his form with a new contract and named one of Iraola’s new vice-captains following the departures of Andy Robertson and Mohamed Salah. Szoboszlai’s importance to the club could not have been clearer, and for many he was - and is - regarded as the most likely captain-in-waiting after Virgil van Dijk departs, whether that’s next summer or later.

But 10 league games into the new season and it’s clear that Mac Allister is Iraola’s first-choice pick in his midfield two, and there are now growing calls for Trey Nyoni to be the player alongside the Argentine.

The pairing of Gravenberch and Szoboszlai was woefully exposed on the opening day at Newcastle, with the Dutchman finding himself very much out of favour once Mac Allister was back available after his later return due to the World Cup. But Mac Allister and Szoboszlai together also appears to lack balance, or understanding of when to press in Iraola’s system. “Both of the midfielders, whether it’s Mac Allister or Szoboszlai, have a tendency to vacate that space in front of the defence because of the press the manager wants to do,” Sturridge noted, accurately.

Injury to Szoboszlai during the last international break opened the door for teenager Nyoni's big break, including his first league start against Arsenal and his first time starting three consecutive matches. The reviews have been unanimous. The player who was handed his debut by Klopp at 16 has mightily impressed.

Nyoni’s first thought is always to play forward, capable of playing quick, direct passes into the attackers and splitting midfield in doing so. Some supporters see this as a stark contrast to Szoboszlai, who often runs with the ball or slows play and opts for a less positive pass.

Nyoni is also impressing off the ball, adept at tackling and comfortable dropping into the defensive line to start attacks from deep. The youngster explained Iraola’s instructions recently as being “as soon as you get the ball, it’s just play forward.”

“Trey is very good on the ball, very calm, he reads the situations well,” Iraola praised in pre-season. “We’re forcing him in the work without the ball, in the press, and he is absolutely doing very well. I think the timings of the jumps are very good. He is always confident on the ball so we encourage him.”

The new boss is clearly a huge fan of the player, who was the subject of a late £30 million bid from Nottingham Forest in the summer and who fellow teenage prodigy Rio Ngumoha says “definitely still has another level to go. You guys haven’t even seen him at his top, top level.”

On the bench for the Palace game, having started the previous three in a row - including away to Fenerbahce where he bagged his first goal - Nyoni’s involvement in Liverpool's third as sub at Selhurst Park underlined exactly what his strengths are. He read the pass from Tyrick Mitchell inside his own box, intercepting with his left foot, before looking up and immediately playing a quick ball out to Alexander Isak with his right foot that completely split the Palace midfield and started the attack that ended with the Swede pulling the trigger.

Two touches was all it took from Nyoni. Technically, it was superb; the vision and execution perfect. It had some supporters making comparisons to Fabinho or Thiago. There is an argument that Nyoni’s passing style gets more from all the forwards, who clearly benefit when they receive the ball quickly, rather than once opposition defences have been able to get back behind the ball.

Liverpool have struggled against so-called low blocks for the past 18 months, since losing the qualities of a certain Alexander-Arnold (and more recently Salah) - Nyoni offers a much-needed solution to the creative dearth.

That, though, leaves a huge question of Szoboszlai - and Gravenberch, with both having signed new contracts this year.

“When a young player in midfield is playing ahead of them, that causes a problem,” Jamie Carragher expressed last week. “Basically, about where you’ve spent your money. It means you haven’t spent your money well enough.”

Throw in reports of Liverpool’s interest in Monaco midfielder Lamine Camara, whose late move to Chelsea was scuppered on deadline day, and the picture becomes further complicated.

Will Nyoni’s emergence as a genuine option lead Liverpool to quell their interest in the Senegalese? And what to be done with Szoboszlai and Gravenberch if so? It can’t be as simple as selling two of the highest earners, but then you also can’t have two of your highest earners on the bench, either. The midfield conundrum could define Iraola’s first season, and it might lead to a high-profile departure or two.

Matt Ladson is the co-founder and editor of This Is Anfield, the independent Liverpool news and comment website, and covers all areas of the Reds for FourFourTwo – including transfer analysis, interviews, title wins and European trophies. As well as writing about Liverpool for FourFourTwo he also contributes to other titles including Yahoo and Bleacher Report. He is a lifelong fan of the Reds.

#1109. EU moves to loosen rules on pesticide use as experts sound the alarm

The European Union wants to relax rules for pesticides, saying it will be easier for farmers to adopt more environmentally friendly options. But health and environmental experts say the risks are far too great.

As part of its drive to "streamline and simplify" EU laws, the European Commission has proposed sweeping changes for agriculture and food safety legislation. These include a move to ease rules controlling the use of pesticides and herbicides, which help fight pests and weeds.

Under current EU rules, which date back to 2011, primary pesticide components, or active substances, are only granted approval for limited periods of no more than 15 years.

The European Commission's proposed revamp of the system would make indefinite greenlighting — including of the controversial glyphosate, which has been linked to cancer and kills almost all plant life — the default. Safety reviews would only be done in exceptional cases, and regulatory authorities, not the industry, would bear responsibility.

The commission has said its goal is to cut costs, simplify work for authorities and help farmers stay competitive. Scientists and doctors, however, warn that concerns over human health and environmental impact from these toxic substances are being brushed aside.

The European Commission has said it's responding to complaints from farmers and the agriculture industry to clarify EU rules that govern pesticide use.

A joint statement released in May by 19 food associations, including CropLife Europe, which promotes pesticides, said complicated administrative procedures and a lengthy approvals process meant farmers were "left without any effective solutions to protect their crops against insects, weeds and diseases," putting food security and livelihoods at risk.

"The existing system of periodic renewal assessment of every active substance has become unsustainable," the commission's press service told DW, citing "chronic delays" and "bottlenecks" in the approval of new, more sustainable products.

In recent negotiations, EU member states said open-ended authorizations should be restricted to "low-risk active substances."

But their stance is still wanting to extend initial approval periods for other substances to up to 15 years, and a maximum of 25 years for renewals.

Herbert Dorfmann, a center-right Italian member of the European Parliament, said there is currently a yearslong delay in approving new pesticides, including more eco-friendly options, meaning farmers are forced to rely on older substances. Or, if these are banned, go without altogether.

The commission wants to "make the system more efficient and responsive," while guaranteeing that "the protection of human and animal health and the environment remain the highest priorities."

Dorfmann, who as co-rapporteur is responsible for interinstitutional negotiations on the issue, backs the commission's stance, saying the EU needs "to open up the system for innovation."

He aims to bring the parliament's proposal on the new pesticide rules to a vote among EU lawmakers before the end of the year.

Ecologists and medical experts, however, have spoken out forcefully against the proposed changes, saying the potential implications for human health and the environment are being downplayed.

In September, more than 500 experts from across the EU signed an open letter calling on the European Parliament to suspend its consideration of the new regulations and conduct an independent investigation into health and environmental impacts.

On October 7, UN rights experts also backed the call for a full review into whether the proposed changes violated the EU's obligations under international human rights law, especially with regard to agricultural workers and children.

Pesticides can persist in the environment, contaminating water and degrading soils. They can also drive biodiversity loss and poison other animals higher up the food chain.

When it comes to humans, the European Environment Agency has said it was "not yet possible to estimate the burden of disease linked to current levels of exposure to all pesticides."

However, exposure to chemical pesticides, including banned substances that still persist in the environment, has been linked to various cancers, chronic respiratory disease, neurological disorders and developmental delays, as well as problems with fertility and behavior.

And exposure is widespread: A survey conducted between 2014 and 2021 found that 84% of urine samples from both children and adults in five European countries contained residue from two or more pesticides.

Martina Vijver, scientific director and ecotoxicology expert at Leiden University in the Netherlands, said experts were "deeply concerned" that the EU's current plan "will weaken rather than strengthen the level of protection for pesticide regulation."

Speaking at the European Parliament in September, she said regular reassessments were key to evaluating the safety of pesticides with new findings, pointing out that the perception of risk changes over time.

"The regulatory system must remain capable of correcting yesterday's decisions with tomorrow's knowledge," she said.

Salome Roynel, a policy officer at the Pesticide Action Network Europe, an NGO based in Brussels, said the harmful effects of pesticides aren't often fully understood until years later, when the product is up for reconsideration.

"New science emerges all the time," she told DW, highlighting how 56 active substances have been banned in the EU since 2011 as a result of periodic reviews.

That includes the insecticide chlorpyrifos, previously used in orchards and on vegetable and cereal crops, which has been tied to harmful effects on children's brain development.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Roynel said it was "obvious that there was some kind of alignment" between the changes proposed by the EU institutions and the demands of the pesticide lobby.

This echoes a new report by nonprofit research and campaign group Corporate Europe Observatory, which said Dorfmann and other lawmakers had "copy-pasted […] industry demands" into their regulatory proposals.

Dorfmann denied the lobby influence, telling DW he had met with "both sides, industry and environmental associations," in public debates on the issue.

"The main objective is not to keep old products in the market. The main objective is to bring new ones to the market," Dorfmann said.

Part of that plan, he added, would be to help more environmentally friendly "biocontrol" products and low-risk substances to bypass current administrative hurdles and get on the market faster.

It's an idea previously championed by Vijver, who agrees that the current system means more environmentally friendly pesticides are stuck in an administrative "traffic jam." She told DW that biocontrol products could go in a green "bus lane" to ease the way to approval at the European Food Safety Authority, while maintaining crucial safety reviews to filter out the more dangerous products.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Roynel also supports the plan to speed up approval for biocontrol substances, but said it needs to be part of a wider system change that includes financial support, monitoring and training to use these new products, as well as maintaining the restrictions on more harmful chemical pesticides ― not further deregulation.

"If farmers get easier access to synthetic pesticides tomorrow, they would have no incentive to switch to biocontrol," she said. "It's important to put [biocontrol pesticides] on the market and we fully support that, but… it will not be the silver bullet."

The former Fulham full-back held the record for being the Premier League's youngest-ever player for 12 years

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Matthew Briggs became an instant pub quiz question in his very fist game in senior football.

By coming off the bench against Middlesbrough in May 2007, the Fulham left-back set a new Premier League record as its youngest-ever player.

Briggs inherited the distinction from Izzy Brown and would give it up to Harvey Elliott 12 years later, before Ethan Nwaneri set the mark at 15 years, 181 days in 2022.

But as Briggs told FourFourTwo: "Being the Premier League’s youngest player was one of the greatest moments and achievements of my life, but it came with a lot of pressure.

"When I eventually lost the title to Harvey Elliott after 12 long years - the longest anyone has had it - it felt like the pressure had been lifted and I could just be me.

"People had always been wondering why I wasn’t doing this and that, why I wasn’t achieving what they believed I should have been achieving.

"It’s a lot of noise to deal with. I have sympathy for Harvey Elliott now, too.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

I actually thought he was doing well at Liverpool, and he’s still young enough to get back to doing what he does best."

Briggs believes that starting at such a high level so young can make the adaptation that much harder if you end up having to work your way back up the pyramid.

That's particularly true if your first move away comes as abruptly as it did for Briggs when he left Fulham for Millwall in 2014in the first permanent switch of his itinerant career.

Briggs explained: "I suffered a lot of injuries, although I was offered a three-year contract extension before I left Fulham.

"But Martin Jol got sacked, a new manager came in and got rid of the whole team – I was injured at the time, and he wanted to bring in fresh blood. I’d been there since the age of 10.

"When you drop down the leagues, you have the aspiration to get back to the top, but when you get to a certain age, it’s harder to do that, especially when you’re suffering with injuries.

"I suffered a lot with mental health because of that. Everything that was my superpower – speed, power, getting up and down the pitch, my body was stopping me from doing it.

"I went to Denmark and really enjoyed my first season, but then my hip started playing up again and they told me I should retire, because I had no cartilage in my hip. I came back to the UK and played non-league for two more years, but my body just gave up."

Steven Chicken has been working as a football writer since 2009, taking in stints with Football365 and the Huddersfield Examiner. Steven still covers Huddersfield Town home and away for his own publication, WeAreTerriers.com. Steven is a two-time nominee for Regional Journalist of the Year at the prestigious British Sports Journalism Awards, making the shortlist in 2020 and 2023.

Arsenal have five first-team central midfielders - but want to sign a sixth

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Arsenal have entered the race for Alex Scott, with Bournemouth softening their stance in selling their prize asset.

The Guernsey-born schemer emerged as one of the Cherries' key players last season under Andoni Iraola, starting the season impressively and earning his first England cap earlier this season.

With a plethora of big clubs interested in his signature, however, his future may well lie away from the south coast.

Arsenal have no pressing concerns to strengthen in midfield, having already picked up Bruno Guimaraes over the summer to compete with Martin Zubimendi alongside Declan Rice.

Manager Mikel Arteta also has Myles Lewis-Skelly and Mikel Merino as options in the midfield, too, meaning that any incoming signing would be competing with four other players for a spot alongside Rice and Martin Odegaard.

Sky Sports have reported, however, that this hasn't stopped the champions from joining the race for the Bournemouth star, alongside Chelsea and Liverpool.

With Scott out of contract in 2028, the Cherries are under pressure to either extend his deal or sell him while they can still fetch a big fee – but would rather not sell midseason, as they had to when Manchester City triggered Antoine Semenyo's release clause in January.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Liverpool are believed to be leading the race, given the link with now-manager Andoni Iraola, while Chelsea are also retain interest from the summer, having failed to land Lamine Camara towards the end of the summer window.

Arsenal will naturally have to sell one of their midfield options to land Scott, with both Merino and Zubimendi struggling for game time this term, with the former speaking out recently about both his and his Basque team-mate's lack of minutes this season.

“We know what our roles are, and we're both calm and eager to keep training hard to show that we can continue to be there,” Merino said, adding, “Not being on the pitch most of the time isn't ideal for a player. Arsenal is currently the best team in the world, and it's very difficult to get minutes.”

Lewis-Skelly could well be an option to sell, however, with the Hale End star representing a pure profit sale, should he depart.

The same Sky Sports report adds that Arsenal are also looking to the likes of RB Leipzig's Antonio Nusa and Brentford's Kevin Schade to strengthen the attack.

Scott is worth €70 million, according to Transfermarkt. Arsenal travel to Newcastle United when Premier League action resumes this weekend.

#1106. Argentina star Leandro Paredes collapses during post-match interview as journalist tries to break his fall after he 'felt dizzy' at the end of the first half of Boca Juniors' cup glory

Published: 05:59 EST, 22 November 2026 | Updated: 07:45 EST, 22 November 2026

Argentina star Leandro Paredes collapsed during a live interview immediately after winning a trophy with his Boca Juniors side.

The 32-year-old was one of the focal points of a World Cup side that reached the final last summer, and went on to win the Copa Sudamericana on Saturday evening after beating Brazil's Atletico Mineiro 2-0 in Barranquilla.

But amid the thick humidity and Colombian heat, Paredes became overwhelmed moments after lifting the trophy.

After giving a brief interview, Paredes was captured closing his eyes, before falling towards the interviewer, who attempted to break his fall.

Instead, the former Paris Saint-Germain midfielder hit the ground, with attendants rushing to help him after his collapse.

Paredes had been taken off in the second-half after suffering from heat-related dizziness, with humidity at 80 per cent heading into the match, and 32-degree-temperatures.

🚨Paredes desmaia enquanto dava a entrevista após conquistar a #Sudamericana pic.twitter.com/M6jPojsZGs

Leandro Parades collapsed to the floor during a post-match interview after winning the Copa Sudamericana with Boca Juniors

The interviewer attempted to break his fall as the former PSG crumpled to the turf

'He felt dizzy towards the end of the first-half,' his manager Rodolfo Arruabarrena explained of the substitution. 'He improved a little during the break, but after 10 minutes in the second-half, you could see he was struggling.'

Fortunately, Paredes was revived quickly and treated in the treatment room, before re-joining his team's celebrations after claiming the South American trophy.

The star shared a brief statement on social media confirming he was fine after the interview aired.

'We're fine,' Paredes confirmed with a picture taken during treatment, before adding in a separate caption: 'Thanks to everyone for the messages, it was just a dizziness from so many turns together'.

Paredes' triumph for his club side comes months after agonising defeat to Spain in New York at the World Cup final in July.

Argentina were felled by a solitary goal from Ferran Torres to end their reign as world champions, before the match descended into petty scraps - with Paredes at the heart of the bad behaviour.

Paredes furiously shoved Spain substitute Gavi to the floor after the final whistle blew, earning himself a punchy 10-match suspension from FIFA.

He faced three assault charges, while teammate Nahuel Molina faced two, and both players were also fined $90,000 (£66,000).

Paredes himself admitted that the length of the ban had put his international future under consideration.

'It's going to be difficult for me to stay with the national team,' Paredes told the media in September. 'Because of the suspension as well, because of (Lionel Messi) Leo's decision. It's going to be difficult for everything to carry on as before.

'I haven't discussed it with the coach (Lionel Scaloni) yet, but we'll talk about it and see what decision I make.'

Paredes' announcement came just days after Messi decided to hang up his international boots, with the talismanic Argentina superstar treated to a magnificent send-off during the early Autumn international break.

'Leo's legacy will live on forever because of what he achieved, for never giving up and for showing that dreams are hard-won, pursued and, in the end, fulfilled,' Paredes added.

Paredes updated fans after the incident to confirm he was okay before rejoining the festivities with his team-mates (Source: Instagram/Leandro Parades)

'We'd spoken in the final days of the World Cup about how the final would surely be his last match, but even so, we weren't prepared for that because of what he means to us.'

Although unable to compete alongside him in their country's colours for one last time, Paredes joined Messi on the pitch in Buenos Aires for his final farewell, and shared an emotional tribute post to his former captain.

'THANK YOU FOR ABSOLUTELY EVERYTHING CAPTAIN,' he captioned a carousel of photos of himself and Messi.

'It was a dream to be able to have achieved everything we achieved together and to have defended this shirt and our country with you, I'm leaving and we'll miss you always.

'It was a pleasure to be one of your soldiers for all these years and I will be forever! I love you buddy.'

#1105. Can we regrow damaged seagrass meadows?

Seagrass protects coasts, shelters thousands of species and stores CO2. But some 30% of this valuable ecosystem has disappeared since the late 19th century. Can we bring it back?

Half a dozen divers are navigating the cold waters of the Baltic Sea off the coast of Dahme, a small beach town in northern Germany. Keeping the roots intact, conservationists carefully lift shoots from a donor meadow of seagrass and place them in a bag.

They only take a few shoots from each spot, which will be planted where the conservationists hope to regrow another meadow. They've already picked out a prime area for the young plants, which need sandy sediment, shelter from waves and currents and sufficient light and oxygen to thrive.

The scientists see the work as critical. Myriam Spicka, who heads the NGO Seagrass Conservation, says she has "seen the changes" in the more than 30 years she's been diving. And she is not the only one who has witnessed the destruction.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Scientists estimate that around 60% of the Baltic coast's seagrass meadows have disappeared.

"That's the bad news," said marine ecologist Thorsten Reusch from the GEOMAR Helmholtz Center for Ocean Research Kiel . "The good news is that the decline has stopped."

Underwater seagrass meadows feed and shelter fish, crabs, shellfish and many other species. They improve water quality and slow waves, helping protect shores from erosion. And they store carbon in the seabed about 30 to 50 times faster than forests.

Around 70 species of seagrass can be found along the coasts of more than 150 countries. Some grow just below the surface, others at depths of 60 meters or almost 200 feet.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Some countries have far more seagrass, particularly in the Indo-Pacific," said Reusch. "There, it can play a major role in their carbon balance."

But the value of seagrass goes beyond carbon storage. Its meadows in the Baltic are among the sea's most valuable habitats. They shelter wildlife, stabilize the seabed and act as natural filters by trapping particles and nutrients.

Planting individual seagrass shoots is painstaking work so people like Reinhard Helbig are trying to make it easier.

Through ZosteraTec, the start-up he co-founded, he helps restore marine habitats, including seagrass meadows damaged by offshore activity, such as wind farm construction. His work begins on the beach.

"Stormy weather helps us. Waves and currents wash seagrass out of the seabed. A day or two later, it washes up here, still fresh," he said.

The collected shoots are grown and multiplied in ZosteraTec's aquaculture. Several months later, the marine saplings are laid on a plant support. A specially developed machine binds the planted strands with biodegradable thread. The resulting lengths can be laid on the seabed with less diving work.

"We plant here on land to cut down on underwater work. That means fewer dives, and we can do the painstaking work on shore," Helbig said.

Researchers at the Geomar Helmholtz Center in Kiel are also testing new ways to restore seagrass across larger areas, including using seeds.

Marine ecologist Esther Thomsen reaches into an aquarium tank and pulls out a flowerpot containing seagrass.

"Ten percent of the plants in our meadows produce seeds. You can clearly see the seeds sitting inside the seed pod," she said.

"The big advantage of restoring meadows from seed is greater genetic diversity. And in the future, we should be able to sow seeds over much larger areas," explained Thomsen.

Reusch from Geomar said they currently "think the most promising way to grow meadows that can withstand climate change is to plant individual shoots as a foundation, then sow seeds between them to increase genetic diversity."

Whether a planting mission is successful is revealed months or even years later.

Thomsen and her colleagues are visiting the first seagrass meadow planted in Germany's Baltic waters in 2021. The divers count shoots, check how densely they grow and record how the meadow has developed.

They then compare it with the donor meadow that supplied the plants. Only that comparison reveals whether the new crop has merely survived or is beginning to function more like a natural one.

"We've just checked the seagrass meadow, and it's really dense. We counted lots of shoots per square," Thomsen said. "It's looking really good."

This article is based on a Global Us video report.

Leipzig break at pace with O’Reilly caught upfield, switching it to their left and running 50 yards towards the City box but Nunes makes an impressive recovery run to win the tackle.

Anderson almost picks up out O’Reilly who had made an underlapping run down the left as Ndiaye lured Baku out to the wing. But Orban stops O’Reilly spinning on to the pass.

Ndiaye rides his luck and two tackles before the ball just skips away form him as he was closing towards the 18-yard line but Leipzig botch the clearance and Foden feeds a lovely pass in from the right to Cherki who opens his body and wraps a left-foot shot the wrong side of the left post.

Cherki intercepts a pass meant for Nusa but goes backwards instead of looking for Foden down the right, killing the impetus of an unexpected interception.

Nusa stretches his legs down the left after a clumsy lay-off from Cherki and shifts the ball inside to meet Romulo’s run between Khusanov and Nunes but Nunes sticks with him and forces him deep, so close to the byline in fact that his attempt to square it goes straight to Donnarumma.

Khusanov, under pressure from Romulo, squeezes a pass that deflects off him and goes out for a City throw-in.

After a moment’s silence for Jesús de Miguel who was killed after being injured while playing for Tenerife earlier this week, Manchester City kick off, attacking from left to right. They are in black with yellow trim, the colours of the bee emblem of the city of Manchester. Leipzig are in white with red bits. City move the ball back to Donnarumma who instigates and attack up the left that the home side deals with easily and when they try again Baku heads Nunes’ long ball away.

City only have a small portion of the stadium for travelling support – but the boos for the Champions League anthem is heard loud and clear. There are a few fans dressed up as sheikhs too.

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Champions League group stage match between RB Leipzig and Manchester City from Saxony. The hosts started the day in 27th place in the 36-team table after two defeats, both by four goals to one, in away games against Como and Real Madrid. City begin proceedings in 12th after victories over Porto and AEK sandwiching that rip-roaring 4-2 defeat by the champions PSG at the Etihad.

City, who seemed in rude health after seven successive wins at the start of the Premier League campaign despite the guilty verdicts in the Premier League’s case against them for financial cheating, have wobbled since then, losing their last two league games. Marc Guéhi and Gigi Donnarumma are both suffering bouts of poor form, other individual errors continue to plague them and, although they are creating hatfuls of chances, they have been thwarted by a combination of imprecise finishing and the excellence of Zion Suzuki and Bart Verbruggen.

For all their travails on the road – RB Leipzig have also lost at Werder Bremen, Bayer Leverkusen and Bayern Munich – they have won all their home Bundesliga matches as well as a 1-0 victory over PSV in this competition. Their total of 22 league goals is second only to Bayern’s 27 and Antonio Nusa, a Norway team-mate of Erling Haaland, is in sparkling form flitting behind strikers Christopher Nkunku and Romulo. City, whose full-backs, if you can describe the centre-backs and midfielders who play either side of the centre-halves in that way, never look fit for purpose defensively and may well have their work cut out tonight if he drifts wide.

The Red Bull coaching principles, which have treated us to the dross football of Jesse Marsch, Matthias Jaissle and Ralph Hasenhüttl, all about the long pass, the central channel, counter-pressing and second balls, have a new proponent in Martín Demichelis, the forner City and Argentina defender who won the title in 2014 at the Etihad. Three years ago he led River Plate to the title in Argentina, the highlight of a coaching career also spent running Bayern’s U21s, Monterey and Mallorca.

These two have met six times in the last five years, City winning four, most notably the 7-0 thrashing at the Etihad in 2023’s Round of 16, the year they went on to win the Treble. Leipzig’s only victory came at home five years ago in the sixth, redundant group game when City and PSG had already clinched qualification for the knockout stages.

Antoine Semenyo is City’s only absentee; Leipzig will have to do without one-cap Germany midfielder Assan Ouédraogo and former Chelsea striker Marc Guiu.

Leicester City have binned their front-of-shirt sponsor aftere a controversial partnership with a pornographic actor.

Leicester confirmed in a statement on their official website that they reached a mutual agreement with cryptocurrency casino BC.GAME to terminate their affiliation with immediate effect, following “constructive discussions” that “recognised our differing commercial priorities”.

This comes after the Belize-registered brand named Russian porn actor Eva Elfie as an ambassador, posting a video of Elfie and a delivery driver on social media, with the caption, “Let the fun begin.”

The Foxes Trust, which represents Leicester supporters, released a statement claiming that the League One club were “ditching its values” by linking up with a betting company in the first place, before condemning this latest partnership from BC.GAME.

“From the moment the club decided to take sponsorship from a betting company we felt Leicester City were ditching its values,” the statement read.

“Now throw into the mix that BC GAME have entered into a partnership with someone who continues to make their name via adult content.

“Partnerships like these bring these two worlds to a larger audience and, by association, link them to Leicester City. Is this who we are now?”

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Leicester have confirmed that fans who bought a shirt within the last 28 days through official channels are eligible for a full refund or exchange, even if the shirt has been worn or printed with a name on the back.

It was recently claimed that the club would struggle to terminate their partnership with BC.GAME, from a legal standpoint – while there may be further financial issues from losing the sponsorship.

This mishap is the latest in a long line of events at the King Power Stadium that fans would rather forget, with the 2015/16 Premier League champions now languishing in League One and making the headlines for all the wrong reasons.

Following relegation from the top flight in 2024 – the first campaign that BC.GAME adorned Leicester's shirts for – the Midlands outfit suffered a shock back-to-back relegation last term to return to the third tier for the first time since 2009.

Life in League One has been a struggle under Russell Martin, too, with the club sitting 11th in the table, failing to win their first three fixtures and suffering a notable 4-0 home defeat to Aaron Ramsey's Oxford United.

Leicester head to Huddersfield Town this weekend, for their first match in a sponsorless shirt.

Fitness is the aim, and Pochettino is the master of the game

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Manchester United made the first managerial change of the season. Not even spirited back-to-back comebacks against AS Roma and Aston Villa could save Michael Carrick.

In fairness, Carrick’s dismissal shouldn’t have come as a surprise. After 10 games, Man United sit 18th. They’re sole league win was at home against newly promoted Ipswich Town.

And, as has been the custom for recent years, United decided to chop and change for the fifth successive time in the period between October and January. Their last five permanent managers have bitten the dust in this window, dating back to Jose Mourinho.

To say that United are a club littered with issues would be an understatement. They splashed the cash to rebuild their midfield over the summer, an area that was in need of dire investment.

Elliot Anderson and Mateus Fernandes were top targets to sort their issues in the middle of the park. They missed out on the pair, who moved to Manchester City and Tottenham Hotspur, respectively.

Instead, they ended up with Andrey Santos, who struggled to force his way into the Chelsea starting XI; Youri Tielemans, a player that in fairness boasts ample Premier League experience and a history of avoiding major injuries; and Carlos Baleba.

The latter joined 12 months too late, but arrived at a fraction of the price Brighton & Hove Albion demanded the previous summer. Even then, the Cameroonian has played just 397 minutes of competitive action due to fitness issues.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

They neglected other areas, however. The centre-backs aren’t up to scratch. Joshua Zirkzee isn’t up to the task of deputising for Benjamin Sesko. The full-backs don’t have the footballing brain to help restore United to their former glory. All of this would be masked if the team was at least trying to hurt opponents.

This is the major concern for United. Yes, the players may not be the most technically gifted. But if they are at least outrunning their opponents, outfighting the team they’re up against, then it gives them a greater chance of securing a result. This is where United fall down, and worryingly so.

It was in August that new arrival Tielemans said to former United centre-back Rio Ferdinand: “When you come back from the World Cup, you don't do loads of running. Just chill.” Ferdinand was shocked as the Belgian admitted that the players used pre-season to focus on ball-work rather than fitness. This has had some positive effects on the squad. United rank top for chances created per 90 (14.5) in the Premier League this season.

317 touches in the opposition box ranks fifth. An 85.5% pass success rate is also up there as one of the best. Rather, the issue comes when United don’t have the ball. This is where they fall down, and they fall hard.

Using Gradient Sports, a football analysis company, we can see just how poor they’ve been out of possession, namely in the key metrics that can prove the difference between victory and defeat when the going gets tough. After all, this United side has covered just 1,066.8km in England’s top tier this season, the second-lowest (19th) in the league.

An average max speed of 30.2km/h is also 19th. A sprinting distance of 23.7km is 13th. High-speed running distance of 65.0km is worse still, at 17th. 375.8km walking is the third-highest. Even if they were jogging into position to regain some semblance of shape, it would be easier on the eye. They’re not even doing that. A jogging distance of 456.1km ranks 19th.

In short, it’s a United side that isn’t busting a gut to minimise pressure on their own goal. Nor is it one that can last the full 90 minutes. They’ve either started matches slowly or faded in the latter stages of matches this season. When you’re a team playing a game every three days, that simply isn’t good enough. The opening weekend defeat at Hull City should have served as a real wake up call.

Now, they’ll be hoping the appointment of Mauricio Pochettino will provide just that. The Argentine is renowned for his brutal fitness demands. You can bet that these United players will have received a much-needed kick up the backside. It’ll be the most intense couch to 5k of their lives. "First of all he made us very fit. Pre-season was brutal,” former Southampton and Tottenham Hotspur centre-back Toby Alderweireld told the BBC earlier this month.

“The way he wants to play - on the front foot, putting people under pressure, a high line, very dynamic play - you need to run. You need to be capable of running and be capable of high intensity runs - the basic is to be fit.

“Every manager wants a good pre-season and time to give the players their ideas and the fitness. But the players are going to feel straight away that it's a different level.”

It’s a shame for United that Pochettino has minimal time to work with the squad ahead of the trip to Liverpool. A meeting with the Reds at Anfield is never easy to navigate. For a team managed by the demanding Andoni Iraola, it would be a miracle if this United squad isn’t running on fumes for the final knockings of Sunday’s clash. They’re already starting on the backfoot.

In time, though, Pochettino will whip this United side into shape. The results may not be clear at first now that we’re past the final international break of the year. With the games coming thick and fast, there won’t be much time on the training pitch. Upping the ante fitness wise is the first hurdle the squad needs to overcome. Steer the club on the straight and narrow, and it won’t be long before United begin to pull away from danger.

#1100. Volkswagen logs Q3 operating loss of €5.86 billion on Porsche writedown

The Volkswagen Group has filed its worst quarterly performance since the height of the "Dieselgate" scandal in 2015. Share prices climbed in response, however, perhaps because the bad news was so well signposted.

The Volkswagen Group on Thursday posted its worst quarterly numbers in more than a decade.

The company reported an operating loss of €5.86 billion (roughly $6.53 billion) during July, August and September. One-off costs, not least a massive writedown in its stake in struggling sister company Porsche, explained the vast bulk of the losses.

The world's second-largest carmaker is battling mounting competition from and falling demand in the core Chinese market.

It is pursuing a major restructuring and downsizing program, trying to bolster falling profit margins, and executives said the difficulties highlighted the urgency of this process.

"The nine-month results make one thing clear: We cannot afford to lose any time. We must act quickly and decisively," chief financial officer Arno Antlitz said in a video statement.

The results were the latest reminder of the pressure on VW — and the wider German and Western automotive industry — to react to increasing competition in China, high costs and practical difficulties moving towards electric car production, and unpredictable and rising tariff burdens, thanks in no small part to US President Donald Trump.

And here are some of the key year-to-date 9-month figures:

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

VW shares were already at their lowest levels in well over 10 years prior to Thursday's announcements, after months of difficult headlines and the ongoing plans to shed tens of thousands of jobs and reduce production capacities.

Perhaps as a result of this, the stock dipped briefly as markets opened and the news was published, but then started to rally as the day progressed.

By midday in Frankfurt, VW shares had climbed by 2% compared to their prices at the start of trading on the DAX.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

CEO Oliver Blume plans to shed around 100,000 jobs across the group, which includes the Audi and Porsche brands, in the coming years though a combination of layoffs and not replacing departing or retiring personnel.

Multiple factors are contributing to this. They include increased competition from Chinese manufacturers, falling revenues in China, changeable US auto tariffs under President Donald Trump, different staffing requirements when manufacturing electric cars and difficulties moving towards making and selling more electric cars at the pace once designated by political leaders.

Up to four plants in Germany could face closure as part of the plan, which has met with considerable union resistance and could lead to strikes starting next year.

CFO Antlitz said the figures showed the urgency underlying these plans, saying the company needed to increase its profit margins by 2030 to solidify its finances.

Antlitz said the operating return on sales was only 3.8% in the first nine months of the year, even before the one-off writedowns hitting the bottom line.

"That is not enough in the long term," he said.

As part of its restructuring program, the VW Group aims to restore an operating profit margin of between 8-10% by 2030.

This year, amid one-off costs now totaling in the region of €10 billion, it expects a profit margin of no more than 1%, compared to prior forecasts in the region of 5%.

#1099. The two things Roberto De Zerbi demanded from Luca Williams-Barnett's first Tottenham start as 18-year-old star eyes new lucrative deal with clubs circling, writes MATT BARLOW

Published: 08:08 EST, 22 November 2026 | Updated: 08:10 EST, 22 November 2026

Having summoned Luca Williams-Barnett to his office to let the teenager know he would be making his first Premier League start, Roberto De Zerbi could not resist a little bit of fun.

De Zerbi cast a serious demeanour and told him he had weighed the options and figured the best course of action would be 60 minutes with the Under-21s.

Williams-Barnett did not hide his disappointment. 'Why, do you think you are ready to start for the first team?' asked the Spurs boss. The 18-year-old said he thought so.

De Zerbi cracked a smile and told him he was in the team against Ipswich but demanded two things in return.

First, that his young star would play with freedom as though 'in the park with friends' and second that he would work without the ball in the manner of the world's best players in his position, such as Lamine Yamal.

This is where the comparisons to Yamal emerged soon after Williams-Barnett lit up the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. Similarities are evident in physique, his fluency of movement on the ball and the bursts of pace, the way they look to play. Even the hairstyle.

Just as Yamal, a left footer, likes to operate wide on the right for Barcelona and Spain, De Zerbi deployed Williams-Barnett as a right footer on the left, although most of his youth career has been spent centrally in the No.10 position.

Luca Williams-Barnett scored his first Premier League goal for Tottenham on his first start in the top flight

The talented academy youngster may not be lightning fast but he has pace and creates goals

He does not possess what you would consider in modern football to be exceptional pace, but he is quick, and his strengths are on the ball. He likes the ball. He creates. And he scores goals.

From wide on the left against Ipswich, he scored within 15 minutes, darting in at the back post to finish, and created the second for Dominic Solanke, with a 60-yard run from inside his own half and cross with his left foot.

His brilliance lit up the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, where there has not been a lot to celebrate in the last 18 months. Terrible home form was the crux of last season's relegation fears.

Here, they rose to salute a new talent, one of their own. One De Zerbi believes has the attitude to match his outrageous talent. Confident, certainly. Aware of his natural gifts and his technical skills. Perhaps bordering on arrogance when on the pitch.

De Zerbi was pleased to see Williams-Barnett, in a seat nearby on the team bus from the training ground to the stadium, watching YouTube clips of Ronaldinho, Eden Hazard and Neymar.

The Spurs boss, who has faith in the power of inspirational video footage, took this as a positive sign. The youngster was relaxed but more than this he had a passion for football and always looking to learn.

'I'm positive about his character and behaviour because I've been working with him for three or four months and I know him enough,' said De Zerbi, whose tactical instructions involved James Maddison operating closely to Williams-Barnett, a kindred spirit in a footballing sense able to talk him through the game.

When the teenager set off on the swaggering run for Solanke's goal, Maddison could be seen nearby urging him forward into the ocean of space left open by Ipswich.

Spurs have prioritised Premier League experience in the transfer market under De Zerbi to create a more mature dressing room environment. Signings such as Andy Robertson have been key to this.

The policy is not purely for the benefit of academy graduates stepping into the first-team environment, but it does help when it comes to setting the standards required in elite sport.

Anyone gifted enough to break into the Spurs squad will have been feted as a star through the youth development phase and well rewarded to resist others trying to lure them away.

Currently under contract until 2028, the 18-year-old has rival clubs circling if Spurs cannot pin him down

Born and raised in Luton, Williams-Barnett comes from a strong, grounded family - which will only help as he looks to assimilate into the senior side

Williams-Barnett is under contract until 2028 but is understood to be closing in on a lucrative new deal to tie him down because others have been circling.

It is easy for impressionable teens to become conceited in this situation. Williams-Barnett has had discipline and time-keeping issues but most at Spurs speak of a young man devoted to his football from a strong, loving family who are sure to keep him grounded.

He was born and raised in Luton, starting out in Luton Town's pre-academy to Under 10s, before Spurs paid a small fee for him.

His father Jonathan Barnett was a central midfielder in Step Three of non-league football, known as 'Jono' and playing for various clubs in the region including Dunstable Town and Arlesey Town and renowned for his passing, set pieces and with an eye for goal.

Although more of a dribbler, Luca grew up with football in the family, polishing his technical skills with his dad in the back garden. 'He is from a very good family and it's crucial for this type of players,' said De Zerbi.

Spurs have been here before, of course, with talented teens breaking through with N17 at their feet.

There was Mikey Moore's wonderful cameo against AZ Alkmaar after which Ange Postecoglou called for patience and commonsense, and Maddison went on TV and said it was 'like having Neymar on the left wing'.

There was Jose Mourinho taking the match ball from Son Heung-min, who had just scored the most incredible solo goal against Burnley and handing it to Troy Parrott on his Premier League debut.

There was Mauricio Pochettino dubbing Marcus Edwards his 'Mini Messi'. Pochettino soon came to wish he had not burdened Edwards with such lavish praise.

The pitfalls are well known and progress is rarely a smooth upward trajectory. It is a balancing act between maximising potential and getting carried away.

De Zerbi is quietly confident Williams-Barnett has what it takes to handle the hype.

FIFA have announced the three candidates running to be elected as president of the world's governing body

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Since replacing Sepp Blatter amid a corruption scandal in 2016, FIFA president Gianni Infantino has solidified his grip on world football’s governing body.

He expanded the men's World Cup to 48 teams, introduced VAR, and has significantly increased development funding for member federations - a move that ensured his unchallenged re-election in 2019 and 2023.

However, the political landscape has shifted this past year, following a fierce backlash against his aborted plan to sell stakes in World Cup profits to private investors. In short, Infantino’s uncontested reign is officially over.

Two football administrators have formally submitted their candidatures, securing the necessary backing from five member federations. When the 211 member associations vote in Morocco on March 18, 2027, Infantino will face two very different challengers.

Here is a look at the two men attempting to unseat him.

Philippe Diallo represents the most direct threat to Infantino. The 63-year-old took over as president of the French Football Federation (FFF) in 2023, and although a relatively recent arrival into the upper echelons of international football politics, he is a veteran sports administrator.

Backed by UEFA, who have spearheaded the resistance against Infantino, Diallo’s campaign is built upon reform and transparency.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Diallo has served on the UEFA Executive Committee and balanced domestic reform in France while overseeing a period of success for the national team and women’s game. He recently implemented a major grassroots initiative in France aimed at doubling registered female players to 500,000.

Diallo has lodged a direct attack on Infantino’s 'solitary governance', publicly questioning FIFA’s strategy of seeking private billions when the governing body already holds vast cash reserves.

“My vision is that of open governance,” Diallo recently stated. “It's one where the authorities truly play their role and the president is in charge of vision and strategy but leaves the day-to-day management to the secretary general.”

From the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), Kohzo Tashima brings a different background to the election. Tashima, 69, is a former Japanese international who transitioned into coaching youth national teams before climbing the administrative ladder.

Tashima’s experience is embedded in the traditional structures of the sport and served as the president of the Japan Football Association (JFA) from 2016 to 2024. He currently holds the title of honorary president. He has also served on both the FIFA Council and the AFC executive committee, earning a reputation as a reliable bureaucrat.

While Diallo focuses on the opacity of Infantino’s reign, Tashima's campaign hinges on a platform of restoring moral authority to FIFA.

After his candidacy was officially submitted by the JFA, Tashima emphasised the need for a stronger sense of ethics at the top of world football. “We will share with the world the importance of fair play, respect and integrity,” he said. He has vowed to make FIFA a "healthier and more trusted organisation."

The 2027 election in Morocco could be the most closely contested battle for the definitive seat of world football in generations.
